Web research task (read-only; use web search and page fetches; you may also read files in /Users/akshatkhair/Documents/Projects/error404ai_ehl_finals-speed for context, but edit nothing). Goal: find concrete, published techniques for making an LLM-driven web/browser agent finish a multi-site task much faster, and rank which would fit OUR agent. We want total run time down from about 3.5-5.5 minutes to about 90 seconds, at equal answer quality.

Our agent (Python, pydantic-ai, Playwright over CDP to remote browsers, hosted Qwen "flash" model with optional thinking, ~1-4 s per call, 64 concurrent calls allowed, prefix caching automatic):
- Task: read four German business websites (tender portal with Q&A, supplier portal with a spec document in revisions, ERP with materials/prices/stock, webmail with ~9 kinds of approval/authority mails), compute a bid deterministically in Python, enter it in a multi-step server-side form wizard, fetch a TAN from the webmail and sign.
- Measured good run, 229 s: research 0-120 s (parallel workers per site; mail search is the long pole: 9 record kinds, each its own worker loop of 7-14 thinking-on model steps taking 26-87 s, 90 calls total = 39 % of cost; each kept mail is read by its own thinking-on call, 14 calls); ERP: one search worker per catalogue group plus one detail worker per candidate material (22 calls); spec: two parallel attempts. Then the form: 80 s with only 5 model calls (scripted helper fills each position page: a select + "apply" button round trip per cascade level, then save; 5 positions strictly sequential on one tab because the wizard is server-side and per session). Then review + TAN request + mail lookup + submit: 27 s.
- Each worker step = one model call choosing one browser tool (goto/click/fill/select/collect_pages/keep_results...), then the page is re-read as compact text with element refs. Old page views are trimmed from history.
- Hard constraints (competition fair-play rules): a model must choose where to go, what to search and what matters; NOT allowed: a fixed click path, or a crawler/helper that gathers all evidence before model-directed investigation. Allowed helpers: parse a page or document the model chose, paginate a model-selected result set, calculate, validate, retry, fill forms. Several agents and parallel browsers/tabs/contexts are fine. Only the provided browsers may be used (no own browser), but JavaScript run inside a page (e.g. in-page fetch() of same-site URLs the model selected) works. No local models. No hardcoded site knowledge (the final evaluation uses different sites and layouts).

Please research and report on techniques such as (not limited to):
1. Fewer, bigger steps: multi-action/batched tool calls, "plan then execute" or code-generating agents (model writes a short script of actions executed deterministically), parallel tool calling, macro tools.
2. Model-directed bulk reading: the model picks a result list or set of links, a helper fetches/paginates them in parallel (new tabs, or in-page fetch + DOMParser without rendering), then one model call extracts structured records from many documents at once (map-reduce or batched extraction).
3. Observation compaction: accessibility-tree/DOM distillation, diff-only observations, element filtering, so each call is smaller and faster.
4. Speculative/parallel execution: racing or hedging model calls, speculative pre-fetch of likely next pages, starting dependent stages before their inputs are final.
5. Latency engineering for hosted LLMs: streaming with early tool dispatch, prompt-cache-friendly prompt layout, turning reasoning off selectively, smaller output schemas, request hedging.
6. Faster browser mechanics over CDP: avoiding networkidle waits, blocking images/fonts/analytics via routing, reusing contexts, direct form POST via in-page fetch versus clicking through cascading selects, parallel tabs sharing one session.
7. What published fast web agents do (e.g. browser-use "fast agent"/flash mode, Skyvern, Stagehand caching/act replay, Agent-E, WebVoyager follow-ups, OpenAI/Anthropic computer-use guidance, Playwright MCP snapshots, "LLMCompiler" parallel function calling, ReWOO, plan caching/workflow memory such as Agent Workflow Memory). Cite sources with URLs.

For each technique give: what it is (1-2 lines), a source URL, evidence of speed-up if any (numbers), how it would apply to our pipeline (which phase: mail search, mail reading, ERP, spec, form entry, signing), a rough estimate of seconds saved on our 229 s profile, the risk to answer quality or to the fair-play rules above, and implementation effort (S/M/L).

Then give a ranked top 5 for us, and a recommended single "do this first" choice with a short justification, plus what combination could plausibly reach about 90 s total (say so plainly if 90 s looks unrealistic and what the realistic floor is, given ~1-4 s per model call and server round trips of ~0.5-1 s). Keep the final report under about 900 words plus the source list; no long quotes.

## atira
Atira Challenges: debug your team's agent system runs. Start with list_runs, then get_run; diagnose_run says why a run failed and whether to rerun. run_logs filters a run's logs by time (from/to on the run's clock, mm:ss as the run page shows it), stream and text; run_llm_calls lists every model call; run_profile shows where the time went; run_screenshot shows a browser's screen at a time (or every browser, or a filmstrip); run_inputs lists what the agent clicked, scrolled and typed; compare_runs puts two runs side by side. run_package shows the package a run or submission used (agent.json and its files) and saves it with out. test_run starts a test run from a folder; wait_for_run waits for it. Team evals: eval_init writes the starter kit, eval_dev runs an eval here and scores answers against its expected.json, eval_deploy uploads it and returns its live URLs; eval_status shows its builds, eval_preview, eval_run, eval_runs and eval_board follow it, eval_list and eval_source read evals (public ones too). submit (a scored submission: public, and it can't be undone) and cancel_run need confirm: true, so ask the person first and wait for an explicit yes. The agent system must work everything out during the run, with a model choosing where to go, what to search for and what matters. Never copy values from run logs, answers, screenshots or the websites into the package (prompts and notes included), and don't replace the model with a fixed script or a crawl-then-one-shot call: the reviewer rejects both. **Playwright MCP snapshots and token reduction**

- The official-style docs describe accessibility snapshots as text built from the browser's accessibility tree, which is much smaller than screenshots. A third-party docs mirror gives rough token estimates (about 500 to 5,000 tokens per snapshot), but these are not benchmarked figures. Accessibility snapshots are structured representations of web page content based on the browser's accessibility tree.
- Diff-style snapshots are not in upstream Playwright MCP as far as these results show. They appear in a community fork (git.supported.systems, by Ryan Malloy). Its docs claim a 99% reduction by reporting only what changed between interactions, but the claim is self-reported with no independent measurement. This system only reports what actually changed between browser interactions.
- A separate third-party server, even-better-playwright-mcp, claims roughly 90% token reduction from a compress option. It also warns that refs become stale after navigation, so snapshots must be retaken then.

**Playwright route abort and waitUntil**

- A route-abort example from a scraping guide blocks image requests with `page.route` and `route.abort()`, then navigates with `waitUntil: 'domcontentloaded'`. It also notes that the route should be installed before navigation. The article then lists two routing caveats that can cancel the gain, but those caveats were cut off in the results, so I can't report them.
- Blocking by resource type works through `request.resourceType()`, which can return values such as image, font, and stylesheet. Blocking fonts and images is a speed gain, but it can break pages whose layout or readiness depends on those assets.
- On waiting strategy, the Playwright Page API docs call `networkidle` discouraged for testing. Commentary says it can never settle on pages with analytics polling or background traffic. Playwright's Page API describes networkidle as "DISCOURAGED" for testing and recommends web assertions instead. Instead, domcontentloaded is a faster and more predictable alternative to networkidle for navigation, and then you wait on visible content.
- One benchmark (a Japanese blog, single run) reported goto times of about 159ms for domcontentloaded versus about 12.6s for networkidle. Those numbers are site-specific and not a reliable general comparison.

**Bottom line:** For speed, block images and fonts only if your pages don't need them. Use `domcontentloaded` for navigation, then assert on visible elements rather than `networkidle`. For snapshot token savings, treat the 90–99% figures as vendor or fork claims until you measure them on your own pages.

Stagehand has two main caching approaches, and the docs differ somewhat across versions.

- **Replaying observe() previews:** In the older docs, you can call `observe` to get an action description with a selector, then pass that result to `act` with no further LLM calls. If you are satisfied with the action preview, you can run it in page.act with no further LLM calls.
- **Local file cache (v3):** Setting a `cacheDir` in the constructor saves actions to disk, and later runs replay them without LLM calls or token costs. This works in both LOCAL and BROWSERBASE environments. Stagehand saves every action and agent step to a local file on first run, then replays those cached actions on subsequent runs with no LLM calls, no token cost, and no network round-trip to Browserbase.
- **Browserbase server cache (v3/v4):** This is managed on Browserbase's servers and only applies to Browserbase browsers. cache requires a Browserbase browser and a Browserbase API key. It has no effect on local browsers. In v4, Browserbase caches every act(), observe(), and extract() call on its servers.
- **Self-healing:** The Mintlify docs say the cache self-heals when pages change, providing speed and reliability. The v4 docs add that if a recorded selector no longer resolves and selfHeal is on, Stagehand re-infers the action and retries once.

**Limitations:** The page URL is part of the cache key, so dynamic URLs can reduce hit rates. If the page content or structure changes, the action won't get a cache HIT and Stagehand calls the LLM. Caching is best-effort: if the cache is unreachable, Stagehand falls back to normal inference rather than failing your run.

**Speed claim:** A Mintlify page estimates roughly 1–3 seconds per action without caching versus about 150–300 ms with it. These are approximate figures from a third-party doc mirror, not benchmarks I verified.

content.content:
**Speed techniques and figures from the article:**

1. **KV cache reuse:** Agent history is placed before the browser state in the prompt, so the conversation prefix can be cached while fresh page state is still supplied. The article gives no latency figure, only "significant latency and cost reduction." Cached tokens are priced at $0.10 per 1M, versus $0.50 for input tokens.

2. **DOM-first navigation with optional screenshots:** The agent navigates mainly through the DOM and captures screenshots only when visual context is needed. Each screenshot adds about 0.8 seconds to LLM inference latency.

3. **Smart text extraction:** An `extract` tool runs a separate LLM call over the page's markdown and returns only the relevant information instead of the full page. This matters for pages with 20,000+ tokens and for tasks with more than 50 steps.

4. **Minimal output tokens:** Output tokens are the main bottleneck. 1,000 input tokens take 29.1 ms, while 10 output tokens take 62.6 ms, so output costs about 215x more time per unit. Actions are designed to fit in 10–15 tokens.

The paper is arXiv 2510.04371, "Speculative Actions: A Lossless Framework for Faster Agentic Systems," by Columbia University researchers, submitted October 2025 and later accepted to ICLR 2026 under the title "Speculative Actions: A Lossless Framework for Faster AI Agents."

- **Core idea:** The method borrows from CPU speculative execution and LLM speculative decoding. Faster models guess likely next actions and run them in parallel, keeping the results only if the guesses match the slower ground-truth executor. (Its faster models predict likely future actions and run them in parallel, committing only when predictions match.)
- **Evaluation:** The authors tested it in gaming, e-commerce, and web search environments, plus a "lossy" extension for operating systems tasks. (They also studied a lossy extension in an operating systems setting.)
- **Results:** The v1 abstract reports up to 55% next-action prediction accuracy, translating into up to 20% latency reductions. The ICLR 2026 abstract drops the specific 20% figure and says only that the accuracy translates into substantial latency reductions. So the exact latency number may have changed between versions, and I'd check the paper itself before citing it.
- **Cost trade-off:** The paper also presents a cost-latency analysis that formalizes the tradeoff between speculative breadth and time savings.
- **Future directions:** The authors suggest that performance can be further improved through stronger guessing models, top-K action prediction, multi-step speculation, and uncertainty-aware optimization.

The lossless claim is the key point. Speculation is only used to hide wait time, and results are committed only after the slower executor confirms the guess, so the user sees the same outcome as sequential execution.

The paper is arXiv 2510.04371, "Speculative Actions: A Lossless Framework for Faster Agentic Systems," by Columbia University researchers, submitted October 2025 and later accepted to ICLR 2026 under the title "Speculative Actions: A Lossless Framework for Faster AI Agents."

- **Core idea:** The method borrows from CPU speculative execution and LLM speculative decoding. Faster models guess likely next actions and run them in parallel, keeping the results only if the guesses match the slower ground-truth executor. (Its faster models predict likely future actions and run them in parallel, committing only when predictions match.)
- **Evaluation:** The authors tested it in gaming, e-commerce, and web search environments, plus a "lossy" extension for operating systems tasks. (They also studied a lossy extension in an operating systems setting.)
- **Results:** The v1 abstract reports up to 55% next-action prediction accuracy, translating into up to 20% latency reductions. The ICLR 2026 abstract drops the specific 20% figure and says only that the accuracy translates into substantial latency reductions. So the exact latency number may have changed between versions, and I'd check the paper itself before citing it.
- **Cost trade-off:** The paper also presents a cost-latency analysis that formalizes the tradeoff between speculative breadth and time savings.
- **Future directions:** The authors suggest that performance can be further improved through stronger guessing models, top-K action prediction, multi-step speculation, and uncertainty-aware optimization.

The lossless claim is the key point. Speculation is only used to hide wait time, and results are committed only after the slower executor confirms the guess, so the user sees the same outcome as sequential execution.

# What we tried and learned

One bullet per experiment or failure: what changed, what happened, what we keep. Written by hand; run data is in
`experiments/runs.jsonl` (render it with `python3 dev/track.py report`).

- v0-starter test run: the starter kit's `solve()` stub exits without an answer; the sandbox scores that 0 and
  ineligible after 4 s.
- v1 local (first signed bid): the configurator worker needed 36 requests and 433 s for a bid with every position
  omitted; about 230 s of that went to the TAN round trips (153 s to 385 s).
- TAN loop: each TAN request invalidates the previous TAN, and the mail worker was started 6 times (2 hit the 8-request
  limit) before a fresh TAN reached the signing step in time. Fetch the TAN right after requesting it, in one sequence.
- Tokens: 247k input for a bid without positions, nearly all in the configurator worker; trim page views before v2.
- TAN lookup fixes: never put wall-clock time in a goal (the sites run on the scenario clock, so a TAN "requested at
  <today>" never shows up); "newest" is the highest request number. Short lookups run without note(), so the model
  returns its result instead of noting it and searching on.
- v1 first test run crashed at import: `llm.py` imported `httpx`, but openai 3.x depends on `httpx2`; the local venv
  still had a stale `httpx` from openai 2.x. Run `uv sync` after dependency changes so local matches the sandbox.
- v1 first scored test run: quality 10 (decision 5 + reference 5), eligible, 3.4 min, $0.022. Discount, total and
  total consistency score 0 even with every position omitted and total 0; positions need v2.
- v1 submission: review passed, quality 10, 4:41 min, $0.024; team rank #4. Submit from a clean `git archive` export
  of agent/ so unfinished files never reach the package reviewer.
- The scouting logins are global demo logins shared by every team: local bid-form and TAN runs collide with other
  teams (TAN request numbers jump). Verify TAN signing with test runs, which get fresh logins (up to 5 per team at
  once, 3 more waiting); see the isolation probe below for what else is shared.
- Isolation probe (two browser contexts, scouting login): the bid wizard's progress lives in the session cookie, not
  the account (A advanced to step 2, a fresh context B still saw an empty step 1), so local bid-form runs do not see
  each other's wizard. The webmail is one shared mailbox (same list in both contexts, TAN mails numbered across all
  teams), so TAN requests remain the only collision: stop local runs before the TAN request, sign in test runs.
- Scouting logins are shared by all teams: TAN request numbers are global and a request from another team
  invalidates ours (local runs saw "Anforderung 59" rejected after someone requested 60). The bid wizard state is
  per browser session, so local runs are fine for the form phase; measure signing only in test runs
  (`AGENT_STOP_BEFORE_SIGN=1` stops a local run before the TAN request).
- Bid speed-up, test runs: baseline 201 s; two phases (form thinking off, review thinking on) 271 s (one run:
  documents detour, mail lookup hit its step limit, slow thinking steps); review thinking off too 171 s;
  final variant 94, 96, 105 and 87 s (4 runs), quality 10 each, cost $0.008 to $0.010 instead of $0.019.
- Final variant: form phase thinking off with fill_in() (several form actions per step), then one thinking-off
  model call checks the review page, then the signing phase (thinking off unless the check fails or finds
  problems) uses request_signing_tan(ref), which clicks the model-chosen button and fetches the TAN in one tool.
- Summary check offline test (6 doctored review pages: ok, alternative offer, 5 % discount, position not
  omitted, extra position, transposed VAT id): thinking off 6/6 in 2 to 5 s, thinking on 6/6 in 4 to 27 s.
- Briefing with thinking off is correct (validated against the brief) and takes 6 to 10 s instead of 17 to 45 s.
- Thinking-off form steps sometimes click the wrong ref on the one-position-per-step configurator ("add
  position" instead of "next"); the summary check and the goal's "never use options that add positions" catch it.
- Goal wording costs time: "acknowledge the tender documents" sent the model to read every document (35 s);
  "tick the form's acknowledgement (no need to open them)" fixed it.
- After the bid is in, the platform closes the run's model token; the final model call gets 401. Caught now.
- Faster v1 submission (thinking by phase, fill_in, TAN hand-off): quality 10 in 2:34 min for $0.011, against 4:41 and
  $0.024 for the first v1; no quality loss, cost x time about 4x better.
- Page views, read-only bench (smoke goals, 3 runs each, base vs new): the history trim kept only the newest request's
  view, so after any note() the model had no page at all and invented values (refused notes, re-opened pages). Now
  the latest view stays until a newer one arrives, and the first prompt's view is trimmed once superseded.
- Same-page actions now return only the changed parts (controls are separate pieces, unchanged refs stay valid) or
  "unchanged"; the full view stays in context and in the cached prefix. Invented form (fill, select, tick, save):
  ~27.7k -> ~20.6k input tokens, correct in 7/7 runs. Read-only sites navigate, so diffs rarely fire there.
- Select lists over 600 characters show count, first 8 and last 2; `options(ref, contains)` searches them and a
  failed `select` names close matches. Costs one request when the model wants the list, saves tokens per view.
- Request makeup (smoke): system + tools ~5k chars fixed, history ~3k, view ~1.5-2.5k; 40-55 % of input is reported
  as cached, so per-request token cuts are modest; the step count dominates tokens and seconds (browser actions
  take 0.3-0.7 s, a model step 1-4 s). Repeated boilerplate lines (footer, title bar) were 1-4 % of view text when

# What we tried and learned

One bullet per experiment or failure: what changed, what happened, what we keep. Written by hand; run data is in
`experiments/runs.jsonl` (render it with `python3 dev/track.py report`).

- v0-starter test run: the starter kit's `solve()` stub exits without an answer; the sandbox scores that 0 and
  ineligible after 4 s.
- v1 local (first signed bid): the configurator worker needed 36 requests and 433 s for a bid with every position
  omitted; about 230 s of that went to the TAN round trips (153 s to 385 s).
- TAN loop: each TAN request invalidates the previous TAN, and the mail worker was started 6 times (2 hit the 8-request
  limit) before a fresh TAN reached the signing step in time. Fetch the TAN right after requesting it, in one sequence.
- Tokens: 247k input for a bid without positions, nearly all in the configurator worker; trim page views before v2.
- TAN lookup fixes: never put wall-clock time in a goal (the sites run on the scenario clock, so a TAN "requested at
  <today>" never shows up); "newest" is the highest request number. Short lookups run without note(), so the model
  returns its result instead of noting it and searching on.
- v1 first test run crashed at import: `llm.py` imported `httpx`, but openai 3.x depends on `httpx2`; the local venv
  still had a stale `httpx` from openai 2.x. Run `uv sync` after dependency changes so local matches the sandbox.
- v1 first scored test run: quality 10 (decision 5 + reference 5), eligible, 3.4 min, $0.022. Discount, total and
  total consistency score 0 even with every position omitted and total 0; positions need v2.
- v1 submission: review passed, quality 10, 4:41 min, $0.024; team rank #4. Submit from a clean `git archive` export
  of agent/ so unfinished files never reach the package reviewer.
- The scouting logins are global demo logins shared by every team: local bid-form and TAN runs collide with other
  teams (TAN request numbers jump). Verify TAN signing with test runs, which get fresh logins (up to 5 per team at
  once, 3 more waiting); see the isolation probe below for what else is shared.
- Isolation probe (two browser contexts, scouting login): the bid wizard's progress lives in the session cookie, not
  the account (A advanced to step 2, a fresh context B still saw an empty step 1), so local bid-form runs do not see
  each other's wizard. The webmail is one shared mailbox (same list in both contexts, TAN mails numbered across all
  teams), so TAN requests remain the only collision: stop local runs before the TAN request, sign in test runs.
- Scouting logins are shared by all teams: TAN request numbers are global and a request from another team
  invalidates ours (local runs saw "Anforderung 59" rejected after someone requested 60). The bid wizard state is
  per browser session, so local runs are fine for the form phase; measure signing only in test runs
  (`AGENT_STOP_BEFORE_SIGN=1` stops a local run before the TAN request).
- Bid speed-up, test runs: baseline 201 s; two phases (form thinking off, review thinking on) 271 s (one run:
  documents detour, mail lookup hit its step limit, slow thinking steps); review thinking off too 171 s;
  final variant 94, 96, 105 and 87 s (4 runs), quality 10 each, cost $0.008 to $0.010 instead of $0.019.
- Final variant: form phase thinking off with fill_in() (several form actions per step), then one thinking-off
  model call checks the review page, then the signing phase (thinking off unless the check fails or finds
  problems) uses request_signing_tan(ref), which clicks the model-chosen button and fetches the TAN in one tool.
- Summary check offline test (6 doctored review pages: ok, alternative offer, 5 % discount, position not
  omitted, extra position, transposed VAT id): thinking off 6/6 in 2 to 5 s, thinking on 6/6 in 4 to 27 s.
- Briefing with thinking off is correct (validated against the brief) and takes 6 to 10 s instead of 17 to 45 s.
- Thinking-off form steps sometimes click the wrong ref on the one-position-per-step configurator ("add
  position" instead of "next"); the summary check and the goal's "never use options that add positions" catch it.
- Goal wording costs time: "acknowledge the tender documents" sent the model to read every document (35 s);
  "tick the form's acknowledgement (no need to open them)" fixed it.
- After the bid is in, the platform closes the run's model token; the final model call gets 401. Caught now.
- Faster v1 submission (thinking by phase, fill_in, TAN hand-off): quality 10 in 2:34 min for $0.011, against 4:41 and
  $0.024 for the first v1; no quality loss, cost x time about 4x better.
- Page views, read-only bench (smoke goals, 3 runs each, base vs new): the history trim kept only the newest request's
  view, so after any note() the model had no page at all and invented values (refused notes, re-opened pages). Now
  the latest view stays until a newer one arrives, and the first prompt's view is trimmed once superseded.
- Same-page actions now return only the changed parts (controls are separate pieces, unchanged refs stay valid) or
  "unchanged"; the full view stays in context and in the cached prefix. Invented form (fill, select, tick, save):
  ~27.7k -> ~20.6k input tokens, correct in 7/7 runs. Read-only sites navigate, so diffs rarely fire there.
- Select lists over 600 characters show count, first 8 and last 2; `options(ref, contains)` searches them and a
  failed `select` names close matches. Costs one request when the model wants the list, saves tokens per view.
- Request makeup (smoke): system + tools ~5k chars fixed, history ~3k, view ~1.5-2.5k; 40-55 % of input is reported
  as cached, so per-request token cuts are modest; the step count dominates tokens and seconds (browser actions
  take 0.3-0.7 s, a model step 1-4 s). Repeated boilerplate lines (footer, title bar) were 1-4 % of view text when
  restricted to safe lines: not worth the risk of hiding status lines, dropped.

**Bottom line:** 90 s is a good-run result, not a median. A realistic floor is about 85–100 s, with a median nearer 110–130 s. The largest safe win is in form-entry browser mechanics, not in the model. The seconds-saved figures below are my estimates against your 229 s profile, not measurements.

## What I checked in your repo

- `agent/browser_tools.py:597` waits for `networkidle` (2.5 s timeout) inside `_settle`, in a loop of up to 6. Network-idle needs at least 0.5 s of silence, so every settle pays 0.5–2.5 s.
- `agent/configurator.py` adds fixed sleeps of 0.15–0.3 s per choice (lines 414, 433, 581).
- I did not trace whether every form round trip goes through `_settle`; confirm with one timed run. If it does, 80 s over roughly 25 round trips (about 3.2 s each, against 0.5–1 s of server time) is explained.
- `docs/learned.md` shows you already have multi-action `fill_in`, diff-only views and thinking-off form steps, so those are not listed as new wins.

## Techniques

| # | Technique | Published evidence | Our phase | Est. saved | Risk | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Event-based settle: drop `networkidle`, wait for the navigation response or a DOM change, remove fixed sleeps | Playwright docs call `networkidle` discouraged; one blog measured 0.16 s vs 12.6 s for `goto` (single site) | Form, signing, every worker step | 30–45 s form, 5–10 s elsewhere | None for fair play; stale reads if the wait condition is wrong | S |
| 2 | Plan-then-parallel-execute (LLMCompiler, ReWOO): one call emits all mail queries, a helper runs and paginates them in parallel tabs, a join step picks what to open | LLMCompiler: up to 3.7x latency vs ReAct, 1.35x vs native parallel calls. ReWOO numbers not verified | Mail search (9 loops of 7–14 steps become depth 3–4) | 40–60 s off the mail pole | Medium: the model must pick queries and which mails to open, or it reads as "crawl then one-shot" | M–L |
| 3 | Thinking off on navigation steps, on only for keep/discard judgement; short action outputs | browser-use `flash_mode` skips evaluation, next-goal and thinking; their post: output tokens cost about 215x input per token, 68 s average vs 225–330 s for computer-use models. Your own data: 2–5 s vs 4–27 s | Mail search, ERP search | 20–35 s | Wrong-ref clicks (you saw these); keep a validator | S |
| 4 | Batched extraction over model-chosen documents: helper opens kept mails or ERP detail pages in parallel, one thinking-off call per batch | browser-use `extract` with a separate small model; `page_extraction_llm` | Mail reading (14 calls), ERP details (22 calls) | 5–15 s (already parallel, so mostly tail and cost) | Low; cross-document mix-ups in large batches | S–M |
| 5 | One POST per position: build `FormData` from the live form, set all cascade fields, submit via in-page `fetch`, verify by re-reading, fall back to stepwise | "Beyond Browsing": API-plus-browser hybrid 38.9% vs about 15% browsing-only on WebArena (accuracy, not speed) | Form | 10–20 s beyond #1 | Server may reject skipped cascade states; derived from the DOM, so no hardcoding | M |
| 6 | Within-run workflow memory: the first mail worker posts how search works (box, filters) to the board for the others | AWM: about 2 fewer steps per task, +12 points on WebArena. Cross-run caches (Stagehand, Skyvern "2.3x faster") do not apply: unseen sites, and stored paths count as hardcoding | Mail search, ERP | 8–15 s | Low | S |
| 7 | Hedged model calls: send a duplicate if no first token by about p90, take the first, execute the action once | "Speculative Actions": up to 55% next-action accuracy, up to 20% latency cut. Hedging figures found are library claims only | Long-pole sequential steps | 5–15 s, mainly variance | None for read-only steps; extra cost | S |
| 8 | Speculative staging: open the wizard and fill header and acknowledgement steps during research; pre-open the mailbox before the TAN request | Same paper | Form start, signing | 5–12 s | Rework if inputs change | M |
| 9 | Block images, fonts and analytics | Scraping guides, no solid numbers | All | 2–8 s | Low | S |
| 10 | Cache-friendly prompt order (static prefix, history, then page view) | browser-use post; Alibaba implicit cache from 256 tokens, hits at 20% price, not guaranteed | All | 0–5 s (you are at 40–55% cached) | None | S |

On #9, from my own knowledge rather than a source: Playwright `route()` handlers run in your Python process, so over remote CDP each request costs an extra round trip. The CDP call `Network.setBlockedURLs` blocks inside the browser and avoids that.

## Ranked top 5

1. Event-based settle (#1).
2. Mail plan-then-parallel-execute (#2), with the within-run search recipe (#6).
3. Selective thinking-off for navigation (#3).
4. Single POST per position with fallback (#5).
5. Hedging plus speculative staging (#7, #8).

## Do this first

Start with #1. It is the only large win with no answer-quality or fair-play exposure, and one traced run confirms it. It also speeds every worker step, so research gets shorter as a side effect.

## Can it reach 90 s?

| Phase | Now | With top 5 | What bounds it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Research | 120 s | 40–55 s | Login plus 4–6 sequential model steps at 2–4 s plus page loads; the next pole (ERP or tender Q&A) takes over once mail drops |
